text: (o) Ποσότητα γνωμικῶν θελημάτων. Voluntatum a sententia quantitatem. Id est plures numero ejusmodi voluntates ac γνώμας, quasi caro suo, non Verbi nutu regeretur; quod Nestoriani erroris est. Turr. Quantitatem vocat numerum; bene id quidem: sic enim passim Maximus, at non quod addit: Numerus enim est quantitatis discretæ. Hic enim Severianorum ac Monothelitarum scrupulus, ac vero scopulus, inde negantium duas vel naturas vel voluntates, quod numerum existimarent quantitatis discretæ ac dividere; quod Maximus etiam atque etiam refellit, ostenditque solum notam quantitatis esse, pro ejusdem quantitatis, cui adhibetur, ratione: in discretis, discretum seu divisum; in continuis sive conjunctis, conjunctum ac continuum: cum sola distinctione, sive, ut alii amant loqui, differentia (Græce διαφορά;) eorum quæ numerantur: quorum scilicet unum non sit aliud, nec eorum una essentia, quantumvis sint unita.
anchorLine: θελημάτων (ο), ἀλλὰ φυσικῶν· τοὺς οὐσιώδεις τε καὶ
en: The Greek 'quantity of gnomic wills' means: the voluntates 'of the sentence/opinion' in quantity, that is, several such wills and opinions, as if the flesh were ruled by its own will and not by the Word's bidding, which is Nestorian error. Turrianus: he calls number 'quantity'; rightly so, for Maximus often does, but not in what Turrianus adds, 'number is of discrete quantity'. For this was the stumbling-block of the Severians and Monothelites, who denied two natures or wills on the ground that they thought number belonged to discrete quantity and divided; Maximus refutes this again and again, showing that number is only a mark of quantity, according to the quantity to which it is applied: in discrete things, the discrete or divided; in continuous or conjoined things, the conjoined and continuous; with distinction alone, or as others like to say, difference, of the things numbered, such that one is not the other, nor is there one essence of them, however united they be.

text: (p) Ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ πεφυκέναι θέλειν καὶ θέλειν. Alterum exemplum est Maximi, ejus quod naturæ, et ejus quod personæ: τὸ πεφυκέναι, esse comparatum, ut loqui, sic et velle, id naturæ: ipsum loqui et velle, quasi utentis personæ: nec unum hæc et idem. Male Turr. Sicut naturæ insitum esse velle et velle: quibus verbis idem significatur, et utrumque natura, contra ipsa Maximi verba et mentem. Nihilque apta nota marg.: Aliquo modo hoc scil. vel illo; quasi insitum naturæ, nempe velle
anchorLine: θέλειν (p). Εἰ δὲ τὸ πεφυκέναι θέλειν, καὶ θέλειν οὐχ
en: Another example from Maximus, of what belongs to nature and what to the person: 'to be naturally disposed' means to be so constituted that, as with speaking, so with willing, this is of nature; the actual speaking and willing is that of the person using it; the two are not one and the same. Turrianus is wrong: 'Just as it is innate to nature to will and to will', words that mean the same thing and make both of nature, against Maximus's own words and mind. The note in the margin is no better: 'In some way this, namely willing, or that'; as if willing were innate to nature.
unreadable: The last word 'velle' at the foot is partly overprinted by a rule; the note ends there and does not continue onto p-0031.

text: (q) Ἐπεὶ τὸν ποιητὴν αἰτιατέον τῆς μέμψεως. Clara sententia; nempe istud vitii ac labis, tribuendum Auctori, qui sic condidisset, quod cum eo natura pugnaret. Nihil bene Turr. Quia auctor esset causa culpæ et querelæ, qui fecisset sibi, quod cum natura pugnaret. Ipse lector, ne sugillandi avidior videar, recognosce ac cense: majorem certe ἀκρίβειαν voluissem in tractatibus sic theologicis. Dispensationis (Græce οἰκονομίας) rationem scite exponit Maximus, ut modum unitionis personalis, qua certa divini consilii ratione, ut nostræ saluti conducebat, innovatæ sunt naturæ, proprie significet; de qua innovatione ad Greg. orat. in diem Christi Natalem. Id sane acute. Dispensatio enim et οἰκονομία, quamdam velut indulgentiam et accommodationem sonat, prout æquitas videtur exigere, posthabito quod ex debiti jurisque rigore est.
anchorLine: ψεως (q), ἑαυτῷ πεποιηκότα τὸ φύσει μαχόμε-
en: Clear sense: namely that this fault and stain is to be ascribed to the Author, who would so have made things that his own creature fought with him by nature. Turrianus does not render it well: 'because the author would be the cause of fault and complaint, who had made for himself what fought with nature.' Let the reader himself recognise and judge, lest I seem too eager to find fault: I should certainly have wished more exactness in theological treatises of this kind. Maximus expounds skilfully the account of the dispensation (Greek oikonomia), as the manner of personal union, by which, by a fixed rationale of the divine counsel, as was conducive to our salvation, the natures were renewed, as the word properly signifies; on this renewal see Gregory's oration on the Nativity of Christ. This is keenly put. For dispensation and oikonomia suggest a kind of indulgence and accommodation, as equity seems to require, setting aside what is of strict debt and right.

text: (r) Καὶ τῆς Ἀπολιναρίου συγχύσεως. Non ita pronum, ut Apollinarii hæresis confusio nuncupetur. In eo erat, quod Christum ut hominem ἄνουν existimabat; sine mente, cujus vices ac officium præstaret Verbum. Erat igitur illi in Christo velut confusio quædam munerum, uti etiam fere Ario ac Eutychi, substantiarum; humana scilicet natura transeunte in divinam, et quasi ab ea absorpta, ut utraque jam una esset essentia, ambarumque conflatum unum; quod signanter Maximus συνουσίωσιν appellavit; cum tamen etiam ipse paulo post confusionis voce Severi dogma, Eutychiano proximum ejusque prolem, traducat. συγκεχυμένη τῶν ψευδῶν διδασκαλία δογμάτων: ubi Turr. Doctrina infusa falsorum dogmatum: pro confusa; quod malim typorum, quam quod manus mentem præcurrerit: et quod paulo ante est in loco Zachar. Et qui habitatis filia Babylonis, pro filiam. Poterant hæc non tantis sordere per Gretzeri vulgantis diligentiam, cum forte Turriano non satis licuerit abs se scripta relegere.
anchorLine: φαντασίας, καὶ τῆς Ἀπολιναρίου συγχύσεως (r), καὶ
en: Not so obvious that the heresy of Apollinaris should be called 'confusion': it consisted in thinking Christ, as man, to be without mind (anous), the Word supplying its place and office. So for him there was in Christ a kind of confusion of functions, as for Arius and Eutyches, almost, of substances: the human nature passing into the divine and as if absorbed by it, so that both were one essence, a blend of the two, which Maximus pointedly called 'synousiosis'; though he himself a little later, by the word 'confusion', stigmatises the dogma of Severus, next to the Eutychian and its offspring: 'a confused teaching of false doctrines', where Turrianus has 'doctrine infused of false doctrines', for 'confused'; which I would rather put down to the typesetters than to a slip of the hand outrunning the mind; and what is a little earlier in the passage of Zachariah, 'And you who dwell, daughter of Babylon', for 'daughter'. These things could have been less careless had Gretser, in publishing, been diligent, when perhaps Turrianus had not had time enough to reread what he had written.

text: (s) Τόπος ζοφερός. Locus caliginosus; sic rite dicta Severi mens. Aquilonis typo. Venet. τύπος ζοφερός, quod et Turr. reddit, facta forma caliginosa: quod certe durum, longeque a metaphora; ut et quod illi sequitur, privata divini luminis usu et exercitatione; cum et istud plane aquilonis locum, lucisque in eo absentiam, metaphorice respiciat.
anchorLine: νομένη ζοφερός (s)
en: 'A gloomy place': a place of darkness; this is rightly said of Severus's mind. [Reading] in the Aquilo print: the Venice edition has 'a gloomy type', which Turrianus also renders 'a gloomy form made': which is certainly harsh and far from the metaphor; as is also what follows, 'deprived of the use and exercise of the divine light'; since that too plainly looks metaphorically to the place of the north and to the absence of light in it.

text: (u) Τῇ δὲ παραγραφῇ τῆς μιᾶς. Sic et Turr. Et sublata una operatione naturali; de suo addens, ut par est, duas posteriores voces, quasi explicationis causa; nec certe abs re, aut extra Maximi subtilitatem. Quod enim ex Severianorum sententia voluntas ad operationem sequatur, vicissimque se illæ et interimant et ponant, sublata una operationum, Christus ἄβουλος erit, sine voluntate, et ἀνυπόστατος, non vere exsistens et in persona, quod illorum sententia, voluntas inferat personam, vicissimque operationes naturales sublatæ ἀνούσιον faciant; quia quod omni caret operatione et actu ac virtute, ut passim Maximus ex Patrum doctrina, id neque est aut vere substantiam habet.
anchorLine: παραγραφῇ τῆς μιᾶς (u), πάλιν ἄβουλος καὶ ἀν-
en: 'By the deletion of the one.' So also Turrianus: 'And with the one natural operation taken away'; adding on his own, as is fitting, the last two words by way of explanation, and surely not beside the point or outside Maximus's subtlety. For since on the Severians' view will follows operation, and the two reciprocally destroy and establish each other, once one of the operations is removed Christ will be 'without will' and 'without hypostasis', not truly existing and in a person, because on their view will brings in person, and the natural operations, once removed, make him 'without essence'; because what lacks all operation and act and power, as Maximus says everywhere from the teaching of the Fathers, neither is nor truly has substance.

text: (x) Τὴν οἰανοῦν περιστολήν. Περιστέλλειν Suid. περικαλύψαι, obtegere, obvelare: nec alio sensu hic verbale Maximo sumitur aut exponitur, quidquid Turr. contractionem reddat, ac si esset συστολήν. Loquitur Maximus de viro excellenter spiritali, cui tribuit, ut nullo spiritalium tædio afficiatur, nihilque tecta ac occulta habeat, quæ vim mentis superant, id est, divina, quæ pro ejus captu, ipsa pene nuda, nullisque figuris ac formis adumbrata, illi patefiant et inferantur.
anchorLine: αἴσθησιν· οὔτε μὴν τὴν οἰανοῦν περιστολὴν (x), τὸ
en: 'Any covering whatever.' Suidas: peristellein = to cover over, to veil. The verbal noun is taken in no other sense here by Maximus, whatever Turrianus renders as 'contraction', as if it were sustole. Maximus speaks of the eminently spiritual man, to whom he attributes that he is touched by no weariness of spiritual things and has nothing covered or hidden which surpasses the mind's power, that is, divine things, which are shown and brought to him, almost bare and shadowed by no figures or forms, according to his capacity.

text: (y) Τῇ κενώσει τοῦ Λόγου. Verbi exinanitione, qua ejus nos plenitudinem nancisci rite ait: τὸ κατ' αὐτὸν πλήρωμα. Mendose Turr. ἑνώσει legit, unione Verbi. Infra quoque, τέλος ἱερὸν ἐκομίσω τὴν σωτηρίαν, non satis apte, salutem, quæ extremum est, reportasti. Est certe finis, non quodvis extremum, sed quod intentum, et in quo quiescatur; quod sic sine addito extremum dicere, eaque voce τὸ τέλος reddere, uti non raro Turr. factitat, non satis grammaticum est.
anchorLine: καὶ τῇ κενώσει τοῦ Λό-/γου (y), τὸ κατ' αὐτὸν πλήρωμα δεχομένους
en: 'By the emptying of the Word.' By the Word's self-emptying, through which he rightly says we obtain his fulness: 'the fulness according to him'. Turrianus wrongly reads 'union' (henosei), 'by the union of the Word'. Below too, 'telos hieron ekomiso ten soterian', he renders not quite aptly 'you have brought back salvation, which is the extreme'. A telos is certainly an end, not any extremity but what is aimed at and in which one comes to rest; to say 'extreme' so, without addition, and to render the word telos by it, as Turrianus often does, is not quite grammatical.

text: (z) Πᾶσαν θεουργὸν ἀποφήνας. Non satis bene Turr. Reddens totam deificatam: vox enim illa activum quid sonat, ac quam Christi humanitas ex unitione cum Verbo mutuata est, divinorum operum vim ac miraculorum. Sic Budæus in Com. θεουργίας vocata ait Christi opera, quæ divinitatem ejus significabant: ipsumque Novum Testamentum Dionysio θεουργία est, ob eamdem causam. Maximo ipso interprete, θεουργικὴ ἐπιστήμη· Sacerdotalis, pontificia scientia. θεουργικὸν μύρον· divinæ virtutis unguentum nempe sanctificans; θεουργοί, qui sacris operantur.
anchorLine: σιδήρου, πᾶσαν θεουργὸν ἀποφήνας (z), ὡς διόλου
en: 'Having made the whole theurgic.' Turrianus does not render it well: 'making it wholly deified'; for that word sounds like something active, and means the power of divine works and miracles which Christ's humanity borrowed from union with the Word. So Budaeus in his Commentaries says Christ's works that signified his divinity are called 'theurgies'; and for Dionysius the New Testament itself is 'theurgia', for the same reason. In Maximus himself as interpreter, 'theurgic knowledge' means priestly, pontifical knowledge; 'theurgic ointment' means the ointment sanctifying with divine power; 'theurgoi' are those who work at sacred things.

text: (a) Καὶ τόπῳ καὶ κόσμῳ ἰδίῳ· pauloque inferius, καὶ κόσμῳ ἰδίῳ καὶ τόπῳ· quo utroque loco Turr. vocem κόσμῳ reddit ornatu. Malui ego mundo reddere, eadem Latinæ vocis Græca amplitudine. Aliis passim locis, Maximus τῷ τόπῳ χρόνον adjungit, quæ sint ea, sine quibus nulla creata possint intelligi, præsertim composita, et quæ constant materia; quibus proinde intelligantur circumscripta. Quid igitur, si Maximus hic mundum pro rei ævo ac tempore accepit, sicque definita exsistentia, quo suum illa mundum constituit, eo circumscripta quasi intrinsece, uti et loco extrinsece? Alius ornatus, qui loco componatur, ad rei circumscriptionem, nullus videtur, nec Græci extra mundum muliebrem ac ejusmodi, facile voce κόσμος utantur: διακόσμησιν proclivius vocant, distinctionis [continues on p-0041: ornatum atque ordinem, qui a creatione accessit.]
anchorLine: τόπῳ καὶ κόσμῳ ἰδίῳ (a) περιγραφομένη· καὶ ἄτομον
en: 'Both in its own place and its own world': and a little below, 'in its own world and place'. In both places Turrianus renders kosmo as 'by ornament'. I preferred 'world', with the same breadth of the Latin word as the Greek has. Elsewhere Maximus adds 'time' to 'place', as the things without which no created thing can be understood, especially composite things and those that consist of matter, by which they are therefore understood as circumscribed. What then if Maximus here has taken 'world' for the age and time of a thing, and so a defined existence by which it constitutes its own world, circumscribed by that as if inwardly, as also by place outwardly? Another 'ornament', one that is arranged by place, seems none for the circumscription of a thing, nor would the Greeks use the word kosmos for a muliebrous world and the like; they would more readily say diakosmesis, of distinction ... [continued next page]
continued: runs on to p-0041 (note breaks off at 'distinctionis' at foot of p-0040)

text: ornatum atque ordinem, qui a creatione accessit. Quod item Turr. partium coævarum σύνοδον ἠναγκασμένην, coactam reddit, non placet: nihil certe in naturalibus coactum (quod violentum usus communis vocat) vera admittit philosophia; cujusmodi est partium illa conjunctio; seu magis coitus, ut Græca vox sonat, ac qua potius naturalis quædam mutua propensio designari videatur. Necessaria ergo illa conjunctio, quippe non voluntate quæsita, sed ex naturæ ipsa inclinatione (supposita efficientis actione) secuta; non ipsa coacta aut violenta.
en: ... the ornament and order that came with the creation. Turrianus's rendering of the 'union of coeval parts, forced' (synodon enagkasmenen) as 'coactam' does not please me: true philosophy admits nothing forced (what common usage calls violent) in natural things; such is that conjunction of the parts, or rather their coming-together (coitus), as the Greek word sounds, by which a kind of mutual natural inclination seems to be meant. That conjunction is therefore necessary, since it is not sought by will but follows from the very inclination of nature (the action of the efficient cause being supposed); it is not itself forced or violent.

text: (b) Τὸ ποτήριον. Videtur Turr. codex hic habuisse τοῦτο, dum reddit: Transeat a me calix iste; quod etiam habetur cap. illo 51 ex majori lucubratione Maximi ad Marinum supra. Nec forte sit aliud hic ipse tractatus, quam caput aliud ex eadem. Codex Raph. Dufrenii et Turr. subnectunt sequenti tomo dogmatico ad Marinum diaconum, ad quem ipsum scripta major illa lucubratio, etsi in titulo Marinus ille presbyter, hic diaconus prænotatur, nihilque vetat eumdem ex diacono exinde presbyterum initiatum esse, quo utroque gradu vir φιλομαθέστατος ac egregie orthodoxus. sic epistolarum dogmaticarum officio a Maximo cultus sit. Ac forsan major illa lucubratio de operationibus ac voluntatibus, cum titulus solum habeat, πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν Μαρῖνον in Turr. codice, ex quo una habemus inscriptam Marino, ipsa adhuc diacono scripta sit, tametsi superior epistola, ad quam refertur illud, πρὸς τὸν αὐτόν, diserte Μαρῖνον πρεσβύτερον habeat.
anchorLine: παρελθέτω ἀπ' ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον (b).
en: 'The cup.' Turrianus's codex seems here to have had 'touto' (this), since he renders 'Let this cup pass from me'; which is also found in that chapter 51 of Maximus's longer treatise to Marinus above. Perhaps this very tract is nothing other than another chapter from it. The Raphelengius codex of Dufrenius and Turrianus append it to the following dogmatic volume addressed to Marinus the deacon, to whom that longer treatise itself was written, though in the title that Marinus is called a presbyter and this one a deacon, and nothing forbids that he, having been a deacon, was then made a presbyter, in either rank a most learned and outstandingly orthodox man; so he may have been honoured by Maximus with the office of dogmatic letters. And perhaps that longer treatise on operations and wills, since it has only the title 'to the same Marinus' in Turrianus's codex, from which we have one inscribed to Marinus, was itself written to the deacon, although the earlier letter, to which 'to the same' refers, expressly has Marinus the presbyter.

text: (c) Ἐκ τίνος ταύτην προσδέχῃ. Hanc nimirum συμφυΐαν velut dicat, coalitî animi necessitudinem ac concordiam: sic enim recte Bud. ex Basil. cui adjunxit et συμψυχίαν, ejusdem seu affinis significationis. Turr. quasi explicationis causa: De quo hanc voluntatem accipis? cum Græca vox significans Maximo voluntatem, sit, τὸ θέλειν et θέλημα, uti et Gregorio: quod utrumque neutrius generis est. Potius ergo συμφυΐαν refert ac σύννευσιν, quod ita feminine dictum Maximo, ταύτην. Mihi ipse reddebam: Ex quo tibi ea proficisci videtur? Hæc enim vis τοῦ, ἐκ τίνος, cum illud magis postulet ἐπὶ aut περὶ τίνος;
anchorLine: ταύτην προσδέχῃ (c); τοῦ καθ' ἡμᾶς, ἢ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν
en: 'From what do you take this.' This 'symphuia', as if to say, the bond and concord of a united mind: so Budaeus rightly, from Basil, to which he added 'sympsychia', of the same or akin meaning. Turrianus, as if explaining: 'From what do you take this will?', although the Greek word that means 'will' in Maximus is to thelein and thelema, as also in Gregory: both of neuter gender. So it rather refers to symphuia and synneusis, which is why Maximus puts it in the feminine, 'tauten'. I myself rendered: 'From what does it seem to you to proceed?' For this is the force of 'ek tinos', whereas 'will' would rather require 'epi' or 'peri tinos'.

Non satis bene Turr. ornamentum pietatis et reverentiæ tuæ: ut nec cum sequentibus ad illa verba, τῇ ἐξ ἀμφοῖν ἱερᾷ συμπλοκῇ, Utriusque cum (illius nempe εὐλαβείας, fortisque zeli seu æmulationis) sacro nexu, ita supplet, disciplinæ scilicet et doctrinæ mysticæ; quorum nihil Maximi textus habet, nec ad ejus intentum attinet.
anchorLine: ἐκτήσων τῆς πολλῆς εὐλαβείας τὸ κόσμιον (d) ἢ τοῦ μεγίστου ζήλου
en: 'The decorum of great reverence.' Here the word eulabeia means modesty, a cautious fear; the very humility and poverty of spirit which Maximus commends to nearly all who referred questions to him, to which he prefaces his replies. Turrianus renders it not well: 'the ornament of your piety and reverence', as he also fails with the following words, 'by the sacred union of both', 'Of both together' (that is, of that reverence and of strong zeal or emulation) 'by sacred bond', he thus supplies, 'namely of discipline and mystic doctrine'; of which Maximus's text has nothing, nor does it belong to his intent.

text: (e) Κιβδήλοις λόγοις. Quod habet Dufrenii cod. χενοφωνίαις, Paulina vox est I Tim. vi, 20, nec aliam forte Maximus scripserit, cujus alterum quædam expositio sit. Latinus interpr. in Paulo καινοφωνίας legit, vocum novitates; Græca et Maximus, κενοφωνίας, vocum inanitates, quod utrunique hæreticorum est, nec liquet quid magis Paulus scripserit.
anchorLine: κιβδήλοις λόγοις (e), τούτων ἀπελέγχων
en: 'Spurious words.' What Dufrenius's codex has, 'kenophonias', is a Pauline word, 1 Tim. vi, 20, and perhaps Maximus wrote no other; the one is, as it were, an exposition of the other. The Latin interpreter in Paul reads 'kainophonias', 'novelties of words'; the Greek and Maximus 'kenophonias', 'emptinesses of words', which is characteristic of both kinds of heretics, nor is it clear which Paul wrote rather.
unreadable: The first Greek word is mis-set in the print (reads like 'Κιβδήλοις' with clipped letters); transcribed as printed.

text: (f) Τῇ πήξει λίαν κατεψυχωμένους ταύτης δὴ τῆς κρυμώδους καὶ ἀφεγγοῦς προβολῆς. Duf. cod. προσβολῆς, ut supra. Haud dubie spectant hæc ad Monothelitarum et Severianorum hæresim, cujus grassationem hac metaphora Maximus exprimit, et cui lucidos sanæ Marini doctrinæ radios concalefacientes opponit. Mihi Turrianus magnopere vagari videtur, dum ita reddit: Qui maximopere frigent in hac frigida et tenebricosa statione fixi. πῆξις, congelatio est. glacies, gelu. Difficilior hic vox προβολή, quam habuit Turr. habetque Venet. cod. vel προβολή, quam cod. Dufr. Nihil felicior Turrianus, dum stationem reddit, quam dum πήξει, voce fixi. Προβολῆς magis arridet, quam vocem optime exponit Budæus in Comment. ut sit quasi pugnæ incursus, aggressio, etc., a cujus significatu nec altera vox multum abest, quod attinet ad propositum: indeque nata earum permutatio, et quod ipsæ parum voces distant. Est ergo hæreticorum ἀφεγγὴς pugna et grassatio, velut andabatarum more, tota in tenebris, ipsa quoque κρυμώδης, quasi gelida, ab Aquilone, quo abest veritatis Sol, nimio gelu constringens, qui eorum afflatum recipiant. [text continues across both columns: forte Græca illa variaverint, aut luxata fuerint. Certe quod hic προβολὴν marg. ascriptum, extra locum est. Erat αἰσθητῶς in ἀπογράφῳ R. Ger. Blacch. sed errore cum feminino puto.]
anchorLine: κατεψυγμένους, ταύτης δὴ τῆς κρυμώδους καὶ ἀφεγγοῦς προβολῆς (f), ταῖς ἀκτινοβολοῦσι
en: Dufrenius's codex has 'prosbolés', as above. There is no doubt these words look to the heresy of the Monothelites and Severians, whose raging Maximus expresses by this metaphor, and to which he opposes the bright rays of Marinus's sound doctrine, warming them. Turrianus seems to me to wander widely when he renders it thus: 'Who most of all are chilled, fixed in this cold and gloomy station.' 'Pexis' means congelation, ice, frost. The word 'probole' is the harder here, which Turrianus had and the Venice codex has, or 'probole' as in the Dufrenius codex. Turrianus is no happier when he renders 'station' than when he renders 'pexei' by 'fixed'. 'Probolés' pleases me more, a word Budaeus explains very well in his Commentaries as a kind of assault in battle, an attack, and so on; the other word is not far from its sense as regards the matter in hand, which is why they were interchanged and why the words themselves differ little. So the heretics' lightless attack and raging, in the manner of blindfold gladiators, is wholly in the dark; it is also 'frosty', as if icy from the north, far from the Sun of truth, binding with excessive cold those who take in their breath.

text: (g) Τῶν ἀύλων φημί. Epithetum est ejus quod sequitur, πατρικῶν λόγων. Turr. quasi absolutum ponit; aliaque non satis cohærentia habet, quod forte Græca illa variaverint, aut luxata fuerint. Certe quod hic προβολὴν marg. ascriptum, extra locum est. Erat αἰσθητῶς in ἀπογράφῳ R. Ger. Blacch. sed errore cum feminino puto.
anchorLine: αἰώνων· τῶν ἀύλων φημί (g)
en: 'Of the immaterial, I say.' This is an epithet of what follows, 'of paternal words'. Turrianus sets it down as if standing alone, and has other things that do not cohere well, perhaps because the Greek there varied or was dislocated. Certainly the 'probolen' written here in the margin is out of place. The copy of R. Ger. Blacch. had 'aisthetos', but I think by an error with a feminine.

text: (h) Πρὸς τὴν ὁλικὴν μετάποιησιν. Ea voce idem Maximus significat, quod voce θεώσεως, ac quod postmodum ἀποκατάστασιν vocat. Fit enim suprema illa animi intelligentis perfectio, quod totus in Deum velut transmutetur, ut jam non aliæ quam divinæ in eo dotes elucescant; uti aliis locis idem luculenter explicat. Non satis placet quod reddit Turr. ad totam possessionem obtinendam, etsi enim quandoque τὸ, μεταποιεῖσθαι, vindicare est, sibique asserere, ἀντιποιεῖσθαι. Hic tamen proclivior ejus vocis acceptio, ἀντὶ τοῦ, μετασκευάζεσθαι· quod beatitudo passionis voce passim Maximo soleat explicari.
anchorLine: πρὸς τὴν ὁλικὴν μετάποιησιν (h).
en: 'Towards the whole transformation.' By this word Maximus signifies the same as by 'theosis', and what he later calls 'apokatastasis'. For the supreme perfection of the understanding soul is that it is wholly transmuted into God, so that now no other than divine gifts shine in it; as he explains clearly in other places. Turrianus's 'to obtain the whole possession' does not much please me; for although 'metapoieisthai' sometimes means to claim, to assert for oneself (like 'antipoieisthai'), here the easier sense of the word is 'to be transformed'; for blessedness is regularly explained by Maximus with the word 'passion'.

text: (i) Τῆς κατὰ σὲ θείας ἱερωσύνης. Videtur hac voce significari Marinum vere jam sacerdotem fuisse et presbyterum, non solum diaconum, quod titulo prænotatur, tametsi ἱερατικὸς ordo, quasi sacerdotalis, etiam diaconos complectatur, qui ipsi sacris muniis fungantur, etsi ut ministri, non ut ipsi offerentes, aliave peragentes quæ sunt omnino presbyteri propria vel episcopi.
anchorLine: σύνης (i) εἰκονίζει τὸ ἔργον, ὡς ὁ κατὰ θεὸν εὐλάβεια
en: By this word it seems signified that Marinus was already truly a priest and presbyter, and not only a deacon, as the title heads it; although the 'hieratic' order, as if priestly, also embraces deacons, who themselves discharge sacred duties, though as ministers and not as offerers or performers of what belongs strictly to a presbyter or bishop.

text: (j) Τὴν καινὴν ἔκθεσιν ἐνεργήσαντες. De fidei Formula Heraclio edita sermo est, sic peculiarius dicta: quam damnante Joanne IV, acriusque insectante Sophronio, Heraclius in Sergium retulit, ut auctorem; cujus ille suggestione ediderit seu publicarit, ut auctor est ipse Maximus Collat. cum Theodosio Cæsareæ episcopo: quam ipsam tergiversationem, qua alii in alios rem sint amoliti, istis suggillare videtur atque notare. Quod reddit Turr. novam doctrinæ explicationem, communis est.
anchorLine: τὴν καινὴν ἔκθεσιν ἐνεργήσαντες (j), ἀθετήτως τοῦτο
en: The talk is of the Formula of faith published by Heraclius, so called more particularly: which, John IV condemning it and Sophronius attacking it more sharply, Heraclius laid back on Sergius as its author; at whose suggestion he published it, as Maximus himself says in his Disputation with Theodosius, bishop of Caesarea: this very evasion, by which they shifted the matter on to one another, he seems to brand and mark in these men. Turrianus's rendering 'a new explanation of doctrine' is the common one.

text: (k) Ὁ θεῖος τῶν Νυσσαέων καθηγητὴς καὶ μέγας Γρηγόριος. Eadem verba relata in Sophronii Synodica, ex qua aucta, quæ hic minus plena videbantur lib. iv in Joan. Ἐπιτρέπει γε μήν, ὡς ἐν σαρκὶ γεγονὼς, ὑπομένειν τὰ ἴδια τῆ σαρκί· Sinebat carnem propria sustinere, ut qui eam induisset. Turr. sibi hic duos divinat, Gregorium Nyssenum et Gregorium Magnum, quem velit Gregorium Theologum: sed nihil apte. Itaque sic reddit, sicut Gregorius Nyssenus, et Magnus Gregorius aiunt. Faveret aliquid, si esset καὶ ὁ μέγας Γρηγόριος, quod tamen non est, nec ejus habuerit codex. Res sane plana, ut mirum cespitasse virum doctum, ubi nec tironi facile obrepat. Est et Gregorius Nyssenus Magnus, quanquam eo forte titulo crebrius decoretur Gregorius Theologus; cujus etiam unus hic singularis Græcis est titulus. In Magni titulo valde liberales sunt, ubi præsertim tanta suppetunt nomina, quanta in Gregorio Nysseno, Patrum eloquentissimo ac disertissimo, longeque eruditissimo, præclaroque antistite et fidei probatissimæ; ejusque denique per Orientem instauratore ac egregio vindice, Ecclesiarum in eam rem visitatione.
anchorLine: Γρηγόριος (k). Ὁ γὰρ μόνος Θεὸς ταῦτα, καὶ
en: The same words are reported in Sophronius's Synodica, from which what seemed less full here is supplied, Book IV on John: 'He allows the flesh to bear its own, as one who has put it on.' Turrianus guesses two persons here, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory the Great, by whom he means Gregory the Theologian: but nothing aptly. So he renders 'as Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory the Great say'. It would favour something if the text had 'and the great Gregory', which it does not, and his codex would not have. The matter is plain, so that it is a wonder a learned man stumbled where not even a beginner would easily slip. Gregory of Nyssa also is called Great, although by that title Gregory the Theologian is perhaps more often honoured; and this is one title peculiar to him among the Greeks. In the title 'Great' they are generous where so many names attend as in Gregory of Nyssa, most eloquent and learned of the Fathers, far the most erudite, an illustrious bishop and of tried faith; and finally the restorer and distinguished champion of the faith through the East, by his visitation of the Churches on that business.
